name: Punica
problem: Serving many LoRA fine-tuned variants of one base LLM on a shared GPU cluster without one model copy per adapter.
mechanism: SGMV CUDA kernel batches the LoRA add-on across different adapters on a single shared backbone; scheduler packs requests onto the GPU with the largest working set, loads LoRA weights on demand, and migrates requests by eviction and recomputation.
num_adapters: Paper never states an adapter count. Single-GPU runs use 1000 requests per workload, so the Distinct workload implies up to 1000 distinct adapters (inferred, not stated); cluster-run adapter count not stated.
ranks: 16 for all experiments per text; Fig 9 varies rank but the swept values are not given in the text (figure-only, not verified).
workload: ShareGPT lengths; popularity Distinct/Uniform/Skewed(Zipf-1.5)/Identical; cluster run is 1 hour synthetic with rising-then-falling rate, Poisson-style exponential gaps, Zipf-1.5, 7B on 16 GPUs
baselines: Same list, but the 70B experiment compares only vLLM (backbone-only, same Megatron TP); vLLM and FasterTransformer are backbone-only, HF and DeepSpeed get LoRA via PEFT; model-switch cost omitted for all baselines.
baseline_versions: vLLM commit 928de46; vLLM and FasterTransformer run backbone-only (no LoRA support); model-switching cost omitted for baselines
hardware: 1x A100 80GB; 2x HGX A100 40GB servers (8 GPUs each, NVSwitch)
headline: Up to 12x throughput vs state-of-the-art systems with about 2 ms added latency per token; 70B on 8 GPUs 441-446 tok/s vs 21-25 tok/s for vLLM
built_on: custom (PyTorch extension, FlashInfer attention, Rust scheduler/runner)
code_note: URL given in paper; repo page not opened
evidence: arxiv html full text (via WebFetch)

name: S-LoRA
problem: Serving thousands of concurrent LoRA adapters on one base model without merging or swapping that kills throughput.
mechanism: All adapters kept in host memory, only those needed by the batch fetched to GPU with prefetching; Unified Paging pools KV cache and adapter weights; custom MBGMM/MBGMV kernels handle heterogeneous ranks without padding; tensor parallelism aligned with Megatron-LM; adapter clustering and admission control.
num_adapters: up to 2000 (synthetic); about 26 in real trace
ranks: {8,16,32,64} sets assigned round-robin per Table 1 settings
workload: Synthetic: per-adapter Gamma arrivals, power-law rates (exponent alpha), uniform lengths, 5 min traces; real: downsampled LMSYS Chatbot Arena logs with models treated as adapters
baselines: S-LoRA variants (no unified memory, bmm with padding)
hardware: A10G 24GB; A100 40GB/80GB; multi-GPU A100
headline: Up to 4x throughput vs vLLM-packed (few adapters) and up to 30x vs HF PEFT; serves 2000 adapters on one GPU where vLLM-packed OOMs beyond a handful
built_on: LightLLM (PyTorch, Triton; kernels derived from Punica)
code_note: link given in paper; repo not opened
evidence: arxiv html v3 (first ~100k of 149k chars)

name: Chameleon
problem: Multi-LoRA serving ignores workload heterogeneity, wastes PCIe bandwidth on frequent adapter loads, and suffers head-of-line blocking.
mechanism: Adapter cache in idle GPU memory (dynamically sized, cost-aware eviction by frequency/recency/size) plus a non-preemptive multi-queue scheduler ordering requests by Weighted Request Size (input, predicted output, adapter rank).
num_adapters: default 100; sweep 10-200 (Fig 20); scalability runs use 500 adapters (Llama-7B, A100), 100 (13B), 10 (30B); largest serving experiment = 500; Sec 3 characterization used 1/50/500
workload: Same, plus WildChat-1M and LMSYS-Chat-1M traces used for lengths in an additional experiment (Fig 21); adapter assignment is synthetic in all cases, so no adapter-level trace exists
trace_public: false/none: only request lengths come from public traces; adapter identities are synthetic (power law, uniform rank popularity)
hardware: NVIDIA A40 48GB (main); A100 24/48/80GB; 4x A100 80GB; 2-8 A100 for Llama-70B
headline: At 9 RPS, P99 TTFT -80.7% and P50 TTFT -48.1% vs S-LoRA; ~1.5x throughput (S-LoRA violates SLO near 8.6 RPS, Chameleon near 12.9 RPS)

name: LoRAServe
problem: Co-batching LoRA adapters of different ranks in distributed serving lets high-rank adapters slow low-rank ones and forces extra GPUs or full adapter replication.
mechanism: Rank-aware cluster orchestrator estimates per-adapter token demand, uses profiled per-rank SLO operating points to bin-pack adapters onto servers with probabilistic routing, and fetches missing adapters from remote servers via GPUDirect RDMA over InfiniBand with local caching; placement recomputed periodically.
num_adapters: 200 (Company X trace, re-annotated); 25 (Azure trace)
workload: Company X production trace (250,138 requests over 8h, timestamps scaled, adapters re-annotated by power law within rank, alpha=1); Azure 2024 trace with authors' adapter names, uniform or Poisson arrivals and three rank-popularity patterns
trace_public: promised: paper says code and traces will be released publicly after acceptance (Sec I)
hardware: Azure ND96asr_v4 (8x A100 40GB NVLink) and NC24ads_A100_v4 (1x A100 80GB); 4 servers main, up to 12
headline: Up to 2x throughput vs S-LoRA (about 20% vs Toppings); up to 9x lower TTFT; up to 50% fewer GPUs under SLO (17% vs Toppings); up to 16x less adapter storage per server vs Toppings
code_note: promised upon acceptance (code and traces to be released after acceptance)
evidence: arxiv html v1 full text; web search (no repo)

name: InfiniLoRA

name: LoRazor
problem: Multi-LoRA decode adds latency and wasted GPU blocks because kernels are sized for the padded batch and adapters are applied for the whole generation.
mechanism: StepTrim releases a request's adapter permanently during decoding (profiled fixed step or learned per-adapter risk predictor) while always applying it in prefill; GridTrim resizes grouped LoRA kernel launches to the largest active adapter row count and captures CUDA-graph variants.
quality_cost: mean relative accuracy decrease 2.89% (1.82 percentage points) vs full-LoRA execution
num_adapters: 128 logical (4 task adapters replicated)
workload: 32,768 requests over four tasks (GSM8K, Spider, MedQA-4, ScienceQA); uniform and skewed (about 80% of requests to 24 of 128 adapters); offline and open-loop Poisson 25-150 req/s
hardware: NVIDIA H100 80GB

name: LoRAForge
problem: Serving many LoRA adapters adds storage/loading/execution overhead; smaller ranks do not automatically speed up serving and recompressing thousands of modules is costly.
mechanism: Post-hoc SVD-style truncation of trained adapters (uniform or spectral-energy budget allocation with rank floor), GPU-batched FlashTSQR factorization, and rank-specialized shrink/expand kernels (RowExpand) with phase/shape/rank-aware dispatch.
quality_cost: At ~7.7% of adapter params, fleet-average score drop 0.80 (Qwen) / 1.20 (Llama) points for LoRAForge-S vs 7.67 / 3.92 for CTS
num_adapters: 85 (35 Llama, 50 Qwen; 20,332 LoRA matrices)
workload: 1,700 requests per seed (20 per adapter), mixed Poisson arrival stream, matched across arms
baselines: Serving baselines are only Original adapters on native SGLang kernels (and native vLLM 0.26.0 LoRA kernels on MI250X in App B.1), LoRAForge w/o compression, and Base Only. CTS (JD-Full) is a quality-only comparison (not served); FLoRIST/SpecTraL/FraQ are recompression-time comparisons only
hardware: AMD MI250X (one GCD, 64GB); NVIDIA GH200
headline: Throughput gains include residency effects (Original does ~840 timed adapter loads per run, compressed ones none) and natural output-length effects; matched-output MI250X control still gives 1.48x. name: VaLoRA
problem: LoRA-based serving of large multimodal models for vision applications is costly and high-latency, with poor handling of domain-specific accuracy needs and concurrent heterogeneous adapters.
mechanism: Accuracy-aware greedy knowledge-fusion packs domain knowledge into fewest adapters above accuracy thresholds (with vision task heads); ATMM adaptive-tiling batched LoRA kernel; orchestrator with one-shot merge/unmerge mode switcher, deLoRA mixture mode and greedy scheduling.
quality_cost: Adapter fusion can degrade accuracy (e.g. fusing six image-classification models keeps over 95% accuracy; video classification fusion drops notably, no figure); rollback enforces per-task thresholds; systems components reported with no accuracy loss figure
workload: Azure LLM inference trace 2023 randomly sampled at varying rates in round-robin for visual retrieval; video analytics with one 30-frame chunk per second per stream; skewness varied by share of the most-used adapter
hardware: 1x A100 80GB (Xeon Platinum 8358, 128GB host); multi-GPU 1/2/4 A100
headline: Accuracy: 24.5% and 62.2% are for object detection and video understanding (Qwen-VL fine-tuned adapters), 45.2% in motivation; VQA/captioning is only +4.3-5% vs small models. name: Compress then Serve (JD-Full / JD-Diag)
problem: With thousands of adapters, repeatedly loading/offloading LoRAs from GPU memory degrades throughput.
mechanism: Joint diagonalization compresses many LoRAs into a shared basis (U,V) plus a small per-LoRA matrix (full r x r or diagonal); clustering groups LoRAs with per-cluster bases for large collections.
quality_cost: Reported little loss: settings with reconstruction loss below 0.6 keep 99%+ of LoRA performance (sometimes exceed it); large reconstruction error degrades quality
num_adapters: 1000+ (quality: up to 1000, paper inconsistent with 500 in appendix; throughput 4 to 1024)
workload: Throughput: simulated random LoRAs, Shakespeare sonnet inputs assigned to LoRAs at random, asynchronous arrivals, 10 generated tokens each; quality uses real LoRAs trained on Super-NaturalInstructions tasks
baselines: Throughput baseline is only vLLM multi-LoRA (matched GPU memory, per-size max_gpu_lora 2-28) plus a no-LoRA reference; uncompressed LoRAs and r-SVD are quality-only baselines
hardware: 1x H100 80GB capped at 40% memory

name: FLORA (Batched Low-Rank Adaptation)
venue: ICLR 2024 (per line, to confirm; fetched page did not state venue)
problem: LoRA applies one adapter per batch so requests needing different adapters are processed separately, hurting throughput and latency.
mechanism: Gives each example its own low-rank adapter and vectorizes per-example adapters into element-wise operations so one base matmul serves the batch instead of torch.bmm.
quality_cost: accuracy comparable to LoRA; about 20% average relative pass@1 gain over base on low-resource languages
ranks: serving sweep 1-8; accuracy mostly rank 1 (rank 4 for Racket, Lua, Marathi)
workload: 1,000 samples from vLLM throughput benchmark (lengths 50-2000); latency tests at 8 req/s (15 req/s in appendix); no production trace
hardware: NVIDIA H100
headline: More than 3x throughput at rank 1 (about 2x in intro for StarCoder 15B) and 2-5x lower latency at ranks 1-4 vs torch.bmm LoRA; advantage vanishes near rank 8

name: PLoRA (NDP pooled memory)
problem: Multi-LoRA serving with 1000+ adapters overflows GPU memory and staging adapters from host DRAM over PCIe is slow and capacity-limited.
mechanism: Stores adapters and KV cache in a CXL-attached memory pool with near-data-processing cores that compute locally and return reduced results; GPU memory manager picks among four LoRA and two attention strategies using a link-parameterized cost model and pre-caches hot adapters.
num_adapters: 1000 (synthetic workloads); 25 (LMSYS)
workload: No request arrival process: evaluation is steady-state batches (decode throughput at batch 32; prefill TTFT at batch 256/512/1024) in a simulator; Table VII gives distributions, lengths 2-430 (LMSYS), 100-1024, 2048-4096
hardware: 1x H100 80GB plus four modeled PLoRA devices (512GB each, CXL 3.1 128GB/s); results from event-driven simulator (SSDSim-based) calibrated against real GPU and Samsung CMM-D
headline: S-LoRA is measured on a real H100 for only two models (Llama2-7B/13B, per text); all PLoRA numbers come from an event-driven simulator (SSDSim-based, calibrated on GPU and Samsung CMM-D); cost estimate assumes $30k per H100 and $3k per device (authors' exploratory estimate)

name: Scute
problem: Multi-LoRA engines reject other PEFT adapters (DoRA, IA3, VeRA, OFT); converting them to LoRA loses accuracy and memory.
mechanism: Expresses each PEFT method as a six-slot LoRA normal form; slots fold into adapter weights at load time, remaining live slots computed per token via fused scale, shared-factor GEMMs or a pre-transform pass; a zero-parameter byte model predicts route cost.
num_adapters: 1024 tenants (64/256/1024 pools, half IA3 half VeRA); 15 trained adapters for accuracy
ranks: LoRA/DoRA 16; VeRA 256; OFT block 32; conversions rank 64 (IA3, OFT) and 256 (VeRA)
workload: Synthetic: prefill-heavy (256 in/8 out) and decode-heavy (8 in/128 out); Poisson or burst; tenants round-robin or Zipf; no production traces
hardware: RTX A6000 48GB (main); A100-SXM4-80GB repeat

name: EpiLoRA
problem: On FP8/NVFP4 bases, separate small LoRA kernels take a growing share of decode step time, and LoRA RL needs an extra bf16 base copy.
mechanism: Launches the adapter down-projection first and the low-precision GEMM as a dependent kernel (programmatic dependent launch), adding each tenant's up-projection in the GEMM epilogue; on Ada fuses all resident adapters into two kernels; RL trainer computes on engine FP8 weights.
quality_cost: served adapters match vLLM accuracy (per-adapter differences -1.0 to +1.6 points); greedy outputs can vary with batch composition
num_adapters: 32 tenants (throughput tests)
workload: 256 requests (512 prompt/256 output tokens); Poisson online; WildChat trace (gamma arrivals, burstiness 0.5); tenant popularity not described
hardware: L40S, H100, H200, GH200, RTX PRO 6000 MIG slice, 2xH100
headline: Same numbers, but add caveats: with 32 tenants TensorRT-LLM beats EpiLoRA by 1.05x on H200 and SGLang is 1.02x on L40S (separate jobs); gain is against vLLM tuned kernels/fastest config; online WildChat TPOT 0.70-0.98x; with default graph sizes EpiLoRA trails vLLM 1.18x on H100 at 16 rps

name: MinT
problem: Post-training yields many policy variants over few expensive base-model deployments; copying or serving a full checkpoint per variant does not scale.
mechanism: Keeps base model resident and moves only exported LoRA adapter revisions between training, rollout, evaluation and serving; time-sliced multi-policy training, PEFT export, vLLM shared-base serving with three-tier catalog/CPU/GPU cache, packed MoE LoRA tensors and two-phase prewarm readiness.
num_adapters: 1,000,000 revisions in packed catalog (addressability, not simultaneous residency)
workload: Serving: open-loop Poisson arrivals over 180s (prompt 1024, max output 64), repeated-hotset and unique-adapter traffic, hot-reload probe (32 warm, 16 new); training on real benchmarks (FinEval, AIME, LawBench, A2UI)

name: DeltaZip
venue: EuroSys 2025 (confirmed on fetched paper page: EuroSys '25, Rotterdam)
problem: Serving many full-model-tuned LLM variants is costly: dedicated GPUs idle, and whole-model swapping adds latency; LoRA systems do not cover full fine-tuning.
mechanism: DeltaCompress stores the fine-tuned-minus-base delta with 2:4 sparsity plus 2/4-bit quantization (SparseGPT-based, no retraining); DeltaZip serving batches the shared base in one FP16 GEMM and runs low-precision sparse delta matmuls separately via a custom SBMM kernel, with a cap on resident deltas and preemption.
quality_cost: Near FP16 on benchmarks, e.g. Llama-2-70B 4-bit+50% sparsity (5.84x) 87.28/44.18/32.87 vs FP16 86.73/44.25/33.18; plain SparseGPT 4-bit drops noticeably (Llama-2-7B 67.16 vs 80.92)
num_adapters: 32 variants default (full-model deltas, not LoRA)
adapters_real: Quality experiments use real fine-tuned models, but the serving experiments' 32 variants appear to be replicated copies of one compressed 13B delta (artifact appendix: 'prepare delta weights and create multiple copies'); paper body does not say whether the 32 variants are distinct fine-tunes. Treat as null/unclear for serving.
workload: Prompts/responses from LMSys Chatbot Arena; Poisson lambda 0.5/1.0 with uniform, Zipf-1.5, or Azure serverless trace as proxy; 5-minute runs
hardware: 4x A800 per node, NVLink/NVSwitch, TP=4; RTX 3090 for microbenchmarks
headline: 2x-12x throughput and 1.6x-16x average E2E latency improvement vs vLLM-SCB; deltas compress up to 10x (abstract), 13.96x for 70B in Table 1
built_on: vLLM (plus Sparse Marlin, AutoGPTQ, SparseGPT, nvcomp)

name: Symbiosis
venue: ACM Symposium on Cloud Computing (SoCC '25), Nov 19-21 2025, DOI 10.1145/3772052.3772230 (stated in v3 header)
problem: Multi-adapter PEFT wastes GPU memory/compute (each job loads its own base model) and lacks independent resource management, mixed PEFT methods, heterogeneous accelerators and adapter privacy.
mechanism: Split execution: a shared base executor serves frozen base layers while clients run adapters and attention locally via VirtLayer; padding-free cross-client batching, no stored tensors for Linear/Conv1D backward, noise-based activation privacy.
num_adapters: Largest serving experiment: 32 inference clients/adapters (Table 5). v3 abstract states fine-tuning of 20 Gemma2-27B LoRA adapters on 8 GPUs; fine-tuning figures in Sec 4.2 go up to 8 clients (Gemma2-27B, Fig 17).
workload: Most experiments use random input tensors, BUT Sec 4.5 / Table 5 replays a sample of the Azure LLM Inference Trace 2024 with 32 inference clients (4 per GPU, 8 GPUs, Llama2-13B), each with a rank-64 LoRA on q,k.
baseline_versions: vLLM v0.7.0 (Table 4 caption); other baselines (HF Transformers, mLoRA) unversioned
hardware: 8x A100 80GB; 40GB GPUs power-capped at 100W/350W for heterogeneity tests
headline: v3 abstract does not contain the '4x more adapters' claim; it says 20 Gemma2-27B LoRA adapters fine-tuned on 8 GPUs. Body: Llama2-13B, 4 adapters (not 8) fine-tuned in almost half the time vs 4 FSDP processes on 2 GPUs (Sec 4.2.2 Sharded Local); no '3x' figure in text - Gemma2-27B: Symbiosis with 8 clients outperforms a single-adapter 8-GPU FSDP baseline (32 tok/s at bs 2, seq 64); 5 clients vs 2 on one 80GB GPU confirmed (Sec 4.1.2); opportunistic batching +20% request rate / +28% generation throughput vs no-lockstep (Table 5).

name: Data-driven ML adapter-serving optimizer (Digital Twin)
venue: NeurIPS 2025 ML for Systems Workshop (9th). Not stated in this paper itself (v3 names no venue); stated in the follow-up paper 2602.24044 Sec 3.3 and its reference list.
problem: Choosing how many adapters to run concurrently versus in parallel (adapter slots) on one GPU to maximize throughput without memory overflow or starvation.
mechanism: A Digital Twin replicating vLLM scheduling, LRU adapter loading and forward-pass behavior generates training data for interpretable tree-based ML models that predict the optimal concurrent-adapter and slot counts.
quality_cost: Concurrent-adapter count: tree models average error <=1.0% (Llama 0.1%, Qwen 1.0%); adapter-slot count: up to 7.2% (Llama 6.7%, Qwen 7.2%); linear models fail (38.6-40.6% concurrent, 17.4-23.6% slots). Simplified single tree ('Tree**') 3.7%/10.9% (Llama), 1.0%/12.4% (Qwen).
base_models: Evaluation of DT/ML uses only Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on one H100; Llama-2-7B/13B appear only in motivation/appendix overhead analyses (Figs 1-4) and the S-LoRA side study (Fig 5, Llama-2-7B).
num_adapters: up to 384
adapters_real: LoRA adapters of ranks 8/16/32 are 'derived from two HuggingFace adapters' (a Llama-3.1 finance adapter and a Qwen2.5 medical adapter), i.e. rank/size variants of two public adapters, not hundreds of distinct trained adapters. Real-system runs are only 882 test runs (1% of grid); 87,198 runs come from the Digital Twin.
workload: Request lengths from cleaned ShareGPT; adapter sizes and arrival rates from fixed grids; Digital Twin simulates one hour per scenario; 87,198 simulated + 882 real runs
hardware: 1x NVIDIA H100 (64GB HBM2 as listed), 128GB RAM, 20 CPU cores
headline: Digital Twin throughput within 5.1% of real vLLM and up to about 90x faster than real time; ML predicts concurrent adapters with about 1.0% average error (slots up to 7.2%) with at most 0.15 ms inference; no baseline comparison reported
code_note: Apache-2.0; described as fork of vLLM for the workshop paper; 6,159 commits; last commit date not visible
evidence: arxiv abs page; arxiv html v2 evaluation sections; github repo page
v_notes: No baseline system is compared (paper defers comparison with dLoRA to future work, Sec 5). Single-GPU only (limitation). Digital Twin throughput error 4.2% (Llama) / 5.1% (Qwen) mean-length variant; ITL 9.6%/9.1%; TTFT 17.4%/17.9%; up to 90x faster than real time. Arrival process/popularity are fixed grids of per-adapter rates (0.00625-3.2 req/s) - Poisson is not stated in this paper (stated in 2602.24044). name: Data-driven GPU-efficient LLM-adapter serving (Digital Twin + ML placement)
venue: Manuscript formatted for the journal Future Generation Computer Systems (named in v2 header); acceptance is not stated. Extends the NeurIPS 2025 ML for Systems Workshop paper (2508.08343).
problem: The adapter caching problem: choose adapter-to-GPU placement and per-GPU A_max to serve a workload on the fewest GPUs without starvation or memory errors.
mechanism: CPU-only digital twin of vLLM-style adapter serving generates data to train ML throughput and starvation predictors (distilled to a decision tree), used in a greedy First-Fit-Decreasing placement.
num_adapters: DT/ML study: 8-384 adapters. Placement evaluation (4xH100): 32 to 1280 adapters (Fig 11); single-GPU Fig 10: more than 500 adapters served vs fewer than 200 for baselines. Max = 1280.
workload: DT/ML validation uses synthetic Poisson (and Poisson/log-normal re-drawn every 5 min, x2 or /2) per-adapter rates with ShareGPT lengths. BUT the placement evaluation (Sec 8.4) replays arrivals sampled from the 2025 Azure multimodal model inference trace (Oct 15-22 2024; random day and two consecutive hours; first hour used for placement input, second hour replayed), with requests uniformly distributed over up to 1280 adapters (arrival rates scaled x1-x100). No real adapter identifiers.
baselines: dLoRAProactive (original dLoRA codebase, proactive placement only; Amax = adapters per GPU, no workload cap) and LoRAServe (re-implemented from its paper because official code is not public). Own variants: Proposed, ProposedFast (distilled trees), ProposedLat (latency variant). MaxBase/MaxBase*/Random do not appear in v2.
hardware: 1 node, 4x H100 64GB, 512GB RAM, 80 CPU cores (digital twin CPU-only)
headline: Reduces GPUs by 2.4 of 4 on average (60%) across evaluated scenarios vs baselines that use all GPUs (abstract, Sec 8.4.2, Sec 9); >2x higher throughput and >500 vs <200 adapters on one GPU; baselines hit memory errors/starvation earlier (Llama: up to 1280 adapters vs 768 for baselines). Cost: higher ITL. DT throughput SMAPE max 5.08% (ITL 9.63%, TTFT up to 18.95%), up to 90x faster; ML throughput SMAPE 4.39-7.46% (RF/KNN/SVM, Table 4), starvation macro-F1 0.93-0.99; simplified trees SMAPE 10.25-12.89% (Table 5).

name: LoRA on a Budget (FRA)
venue: arXiv preprint formatted with workshop title 'Neural Network Artifacts as a New Data Modality' (host conference not named; acceptance not stated).
problem: Compressing a fleet of LoRA adapters under a shared rank budget requires allocating rank across layers and adapters without knowing functional tolerance.
mechanism: Functional Rank Allocation: measures per-module truncation risk end to end via JS divergence on unlabeled prompts, solves layer-rank allocation by dynamic programming, remeasures candidates, then does minimax allocation across adapters.
quality_cost: First-pass misread table signs (leading dash in text extraction is a formatting artifact; the HTML math alttext gives positive values). Mean retention is high: LoRA Land FRA 0.985 (moderate), 0.963 (binding), 0.907 (severe); worst-case 0.931/0.879/0.620; p10 0.949/0.915/0.692. Uniform baseline binding: mean 0.725, p10 0.010, worst -0.293. Lots-of-LoRAs binding worst: Uniform 0.542 -> FuncDP 0.800 -> FRA 0.910. LoRARetriever binding worst FuncDP 0.250 -> FRA 0.500. Retention=1 means full adapter gain preserved; negative values only for worst-case baselines.
num_adapters: 78 total (12, 25, 41 per fleet)
workload: none; offline task scoring at fixed fleet budgets
hardware: One GH200; calibration about 8 minutes per adapter (512 single-layer probes on LoRA Land, L=64, r=8), paid once at registration.
headline: Binding budget worst-case retention rises from -0.293 (Uniform) to 0.879 (FRA) on LoRA Land

name: SwiftDiffusion
problem: Text-to-image workflows with ControlNets and LoRAs add loading and compute latency growing with each add-on.
mechanism: ControlNet-as-a-Service on separate scaled GPUs with caching and parallel execution with UNet; bounded asynchronous LoRA loading overlapping the first k LoRA-free denoising steps then in-place merge; latent parallelism across two GPUs; CUDA Graphs and fused kernels.
quality_cost: Clarify: FID/LPIPS/SSIM are measured against Diffusers images as ground truth; SwiftDiffusion FID 0.53 / LPIPS 0.26 / SSIM 0.74 (papercut, one LoRA) and 0.78/0.29/0.75 (two LoRAs) vs Nirvana-10 2.66/0.57/0.42 and 2.19/0.57/0.48; CLIP 33.9 (1 LoRA) and 33.7 (2 LoRAs) vs Diffusers 34.3/33.9. Pipelined ControlNet (low-bandwidth) FID 0.45, CLIP 34.6 vs sync 34.1, LPIPS 0.33 vs 0.28, SSIM 0.71 vs 0.75. ControlNet-as-a-Service on fast links is exact (identical images).
num_adapters: Production trace: 141 ControlNets (47+94), ~6,908 and 7,463 LoRAs; eval runs use 1-3 ControlNets and 1-2 LoRAs

mechanism: Unified PET representation, an inference engine that batches queries across tasks running shared task-agnostic operators plus task-specific PET operators, coordinated batching, and PET operator stream scheduling.

name: dLoRA
problem: LoRA serving needs to choose between merged and unmerged adapter inference and suffers load imbalance from skewed requests and autoregressive length variance.
mechanism: Credit-based batching dynamically merges/unmerges adapters with the base model; request-adapter co-migration (ILP-based) balances load across replicas.
adapters_real: Confirmed null: paper never states whether adapters are trained or synthetic; models are called 'LoRA Llama-2 models' with rank 8.
workload: ShareGPT content; arrivals from Azure Functions 2019 (MAF1) and 2021 (MAF2) traces, functions sorted by frequency and mapped round-robin to adapters, skewness = functions per group (4-32)

It appears only in Sec 7.7, on a single A800 serving 8 Llama-2-7B LoRA models under the Sec 7.3 skewness sweep (up to 1.8x lower average latency). Merged-only/unmerged-only are Sec 7.3 ablations (single GPU, 8 adapters); RR/Proactive-dispatch are Sec 7.4 ablations (single 8-GPU server).

name: Toppings (CaraServe)
problem: Multi-adapter serving suffers GPU cold-start delays on adapter load and latency variance from batching heterogeneous ranks.
mechanism: CPU LoRA processes start prefill while the adapter loads to GPU, with sync-free fused-operator coordination, shared memory, and profiling-guided CPU parallelization; rank-aware scheduler uses linear latency models to route requests across servers.
base_models: ATC'25 version: Llama2-7B (1xA100) and Llama2-70B (4xA100, TP) only. arXiv v1 (CaraServe) evaluates Llama2-7B/13B/70B (its intro text says 7B/30B/70B - internally inconsistent). No 30B in either evaluation.
num_adapters: 128, 256, 512 per server (production-scaled); 200 typical synthetic; 40,000 functions in cluster simulation
ranks: 32, 64, 256 across setups; four ranks in cluster runs
workload: Add: synthetic workload is Poisson with each request targeting a distinct adapter (so every request incurs loading), 200 adapters per server (50 in S4/QMSum, rank 256), setups S1-S6 (7B: RPS 9/6/9/3; 70B: RPS 3); scaled MAF: 128/256/512 adapters per server at 1.5/3.6/7.7 RPS, rank 64, random grouping with popularity proportional to invocation frequency. Rates 3/6/9 req/s are correct for S1-S6 7B (S4 3, 70B 3).
baselines: ATC'25: single-server baselines are CACHED (all adapters pre-cached, unlimited GPU memory), S-LoRA and dLoRA; cluster baselines are dLoRA (reactive migration), FirstFit and Random. HF-PEFT and Punica are not evaluated baselines (Punica's BGMV kernel is adopted by Toppings/CACHED; HF-PEFT is used only to define the SLO in arXiv v1). arXiv v1 baselines are Cached and OnDmd.
hardware: ATC'25: A100 only (1 GPU for 7B, 4 for 70B), plus an 8-instance Llama2-7B testbed and a 60-instance simulation. A10 GPUs (and 2xA10 for 13B) appear only in arXiv v1 (CaraServe).

name: ELORA (preprint FastLibra)
problem: vLLM-style systems split HBM statically between LoRAs and KV caches with separate LRU, producing invalid cached KVs (KV unusable without its LoRA) and higher TTFT under shifting load.
mechanism: Dependency-aware unified cache manager (tree with LoRAs on second layer, swap out leaves/in roots) plus a swapper running every 100 ms with 95%/70% HBM thresholds and a cost model (LoRA reward x transfer cost x visit probability x recency).
base_models: HPCA'26 ELORA: Llama3-8B, Llama2-34B, Llama3-70B on 1/4/8 H800s. The arXiv v1 (FastLibra) numbers (Llama-7B/13B/34B on NPUs) belong to a different revision of the work.
num_adapters: Main: 20/50/100 LoRAs per base model (3 models x 3 counts x 3 scenarios). Scalability: 1,000 and 2,000 LoRAs on Llama2-34B in the chatbot scenario (HPCA Sec VIII-I; arXiv v1 used Llama-7B).
adapters_real: LoRAs are randomly selected from HuggingFace repositories of the corresponding LLMs (real downloaded adapters), ranks 32 or 64; the first pass's 'synthetic' is not supported by the HPCA text (arXiv v1 does not state either way).
workload: LMSYS-33k chatbot scaled; OPUS-100 and Taskmaster with arrival timing from Microsoft Azure Functions trace (top-n functions mapped to n LoRAs)
baseline_versions: Still no version number (reference is the vLLM repo). Configuration: vLLM with Punica SGMV kernels, prefix caching, static GPU memory partition with LoRA ratio 0.2, LRU swap-out; S-LoRA with unified pool, no history-KV reuse, on-demand LoRA swap-in. An 'oracle vLLM' (ratio brute-forced in 0.05 steps) is still 38.7%/24.4% worse TTFT/TPOT than ELORA. SGLang and TensorRT-LLM were excluded (SGLang cannot reuse KV when multi-LoRA enabled, TTFT 9568.9 ms; TRT-LLM needs pre-compiled LoRAs).
hardware: HPCA'26 main platform: 8x NVIDIA H800-80GB (PCIe 5.0, 128 GB/s), Intel Xeon Platinum 8480CL, 256GB. Four in-house NPUs (256 TFLOPS, 64GB) only in the Sec VIII-K scalability study with Llama2-34B (avg TTFT -69.8%, TPOT -38.4% vs vLLM; -49.4%/-26.2% vs S-LoRA).
headline: The two sets of numbers come from different revisions, not an inconsistency: arXiv v1 (FastLibra, NPUs) has 63.4/40.1/35.2 and 60.3/33.9/1.7x; HPCA'26 ELORA (GPUs) reports TTFT -45.7%, TPOT -37.8%, supported peak load +78.9% vs vLLM (abstract/conclusion quote only 45.7/37.8 'vs state of the art'), and vs S-LoRA -43.3%/-31.4%/+49.9%; P99/P95 TTFT -73.8/-76.1% vs vLLM. Peak load = max QPS with TTFT below 500 ms.

name: M-LoRA
problem: FCFS scheduling in multi-LoRA serving causes long queuing delays and heavy adapter memory use that shrinks KV cache space, lowering concurrency and throughput on a single GPU.
mechanism: Multi-LoRA length predictor estimates output length and KV demand; memory-aware speculative scheduler (ILP via OR-Tools) dispatches requests under a GPU memory budget; recovery mechanism fixes mispredictions by recomputation or CPU-load.
num_adapters: 200 (scalability; 20 in end-to-end)
workload: Prompt/output lengths from LMSYS-Chat-1M (25 LLMs mapped round-robin to adapters), arrivals sampled from Chatbot Arena and scaled, 4-24 req/s
headline: Up to 87% lower average per-token latency (74.6% vs vLLM, 87.5% vs Punica, 85.6% vs S-LoRA) and up to 1.7x throughput (1.4x/1.6x/1.7x)
built_on: PyTorch with S-LoRA Unified Memory (framework not named)

name: LoRA-Inlaid
problem: Standard quantization stops one base model being shared across LoRA adapters, and serving systems cannot add tasks dynamically or account for per-task workload differences.
mechanism: MLGPTQ multi-task quantization lets one quantized base serve many adapters and accept new ones online; a scheduler combines output-length prediction with task grouping to cut memory use and adapter switching.
quality_cost: Average accuracy drop at 4-bit: MLGPTQ 1.70% vs GPTQ-tweaked 4.72%, AWQ-tweaked 4.50%, RTN 4.02%
num_adapters: Max 1000 tasks (Table 3, LLaMA2-7B on RTX 4090; vLLM OOM from 5 tasks, S-LoRA runs). Main end-to-end Fig 6 varies the task count T (annotated OOM points include S-LoRA T=5 and T=100 for 13B, vLLM T=4); the exact T grid is not machine-readable from the PDF text, so num_adapters_main is null.
adapters_real: Mixed: accuracy tests use 12 open-source fine-tuned task models; efficiency tests 'simulate' diverse serving with LoRA adapters of ranks 8/16/32/64 across tasks following S-LoRA, with no statement that the up-to-1000 serving adapters are distinct trained adapters.
workload: Gamma-process arrivals following vLLM/S-LoRA, 0-30 req/s, 1-minute runs, 6s SLO; per-task popularity skew not described; accuracy uses open-source task fine-tuned models

General (Table 2): LoRA-Switch 60.12 vs base 59.10, LoRA 59.64 (+0.48), MoRAL 60.22 (-0.10), PESC 60.45 (-0.33). Ablations (Tables 5/6) show 16 experts lowers accuracy.

name: SALT (Pin Once, Swap Light)
problem: Multi-tenant LoRA serving trades accuracy (high rank) against VRAM/PCIe swapping cost; ultra-low-rank (r<=2) adapters lose accuracy.
mechanism: Provider trains a high-rank (r=16) domain centroid jointly with task adapters using cosine alignment regularizer; each user trains only an ultra-low-rank residual (r<=2) with frozen centroid; serving pins the centroid in VRAM and swaps residuals, with an activation-profiling router and binned scale factor gamma.
quality_cost: Trained approximation; claims up to 18.5% absolute accuracy gain over compression baselines; AQuA below standard LoRA (e.g. -5.3 at r=2, -6.3 at r=4 on Mistral); mixing unrelated domains degrades accuracy
num_adapters: 16-512 concurrent in serving experiments
adapters_real: Real (trained) adapters for the accuracy experiments (GSM8K, SVAMP, MBPP, Spider etc.). For the vLLM throughput experiments (16-512 concurrent adapters) the paper does not say how the adapters were created/replicated; treat as null for serving.

name: Predictive-LoRA (P-LoRA)
problem: Serverless multi-LoRA serving suffers cold-start latency from reactive adapter loading and GPU memory fragmentation from swapping.
mechanism: LSTM traffic predictor drives proactive adapter prefetching with double buffering; eviction score mixes recency, frequency and predicted probability; adapter weights stored in fixed-size pages (default 2MB) with per-adapter page tables.
num_adapters: 1000 (throughput result; not fully specified elsewhere)
workload: Azure Functions-derived traces, each function ID mapped to one adapter, rates scaled 10-500 req/s; lengths from ShareGPT

headline: Confirmed. Add: fragmentation baseline block allocator 35%; cold start median 68 ms to 22 ms (68%) on Llama2-7B; numbers are single-GPU unless noted; ablation gives 50% latency reduction vs a vLLM-based baseline

name: EdgeLoRA

mechanism: Adaptive adapter selection with a multi-label router preferring cached adapters, LRU adapter cache with pre-allocated memory pool, and batched LoRA inference grouping same-adapter requests.

name: LayerLoom
venue: arXiv preprint 2026 (ICML-style template, no acceptance stated)
problem: LoRA co-serving runtimes schedule backward work per serving iteration, so fine-tuning dictates inference latency under bursts (FlexLLM joint SLO falls from >=99% alone to 1.5-19.0%)
mechanism: Layer-granular scheduling: backward tasks of a LoRA microbatch are attached to the inference forward pass per layer; wavefront of staggered microbatches; greedy SLO-aware scheduler using a profiled latency model; scheduler-guided host-memory offloading; fused shared-weight kernel (one read of each base weight for forward and backward GEMMs)
compat: n/a (co-serving of fine-tuning and inference of one LoRA; same category as FlexLLM)
